extracted.intended_audience: psychology researchers and meta-analysts studying well‑being and physical health outcomes
extracted.subtask_description: Conducting and reporting a meta-analysis of the association between subjective well‑being (and ill‑being) and objective physical/physiological health outcomes, including tests of moderators and interpretation of effect sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study design classification and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify primary studies into three designs: experimental, ambulatory, and longitudinal; experimental procedures provide the only direct test of causal pathways and often show the largest effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because experimental manipulations control extraneous variables, analyses were performed both combining the three designs and with experimental studies alone. Report average effect sizes separately by design and treat study design as an important moderator (see QBET tests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect size metric and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Pearson r effect sizes to represent associations between well‑being (or ill‑being) and health outcomes; report both random‑effects and fixed‑effects mean r, 95% CI, and Z‑values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present unweighted mean r and specify which model (random vs fixed) is being reported. Indicate direction (positive values indicate enhanced health outcomes; negative values indicate compromised health outcomes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for random effects for generalizability
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on random‑effects models when making generalizable inferences across studies; report fixed‑effects as supplementary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although both models may be reported, emphasize random effects as the more generalizable estimate. Note that meta‑regression of continuous moderators is necessarily a fixed‑effects procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogeneity and heterogeneity testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use omnibus homogeneity tests (Q and Qw) to assess within‑group heterogeneity across independent samples; significant Q indicates substantial heterogeneity meriting moderator analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report Q‑values and p‑values. If Q indicates heterogeneity (e.g., Qw[211]=903.88, p<0.001), examine moderators to explain variation in effect sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderator inclusion rule (sample size threshold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only test moderators when the specific outcome was reported in 10 or more independent samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For exact health outcomes, moderators were only examined via meta‑regression or subgroup analyses if K ≥ 10; when fewer than 10 independent studies exist, document the most commonly reported exact outcome rather than running formal moderator tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorical moderators to examine
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine categorical moderators including (a) health status of the sample at baseline (healthy vs unhealthy), (b) exact type of health outcome measured (e.g., sIgA, heart rate), and (c) operational definition of well‑being (state vs trait).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrate moderating effects by reporting descriptive and inferential statistics for each level. Example: state measures often show larger short‑term immune effects than trait measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous moderators and meta‑regression
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine continuous moderators such as average age of the sample and percent male respondents using meta‑regression analyses; interpret the slope (b1) to assess association with effect sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta‑regressions are fixed‑effects analyses. Report parameter estimates, SE, Z, and 95% CI for b0 and b1; present QModel and p for the model. Example: percent male moderated long‑term healthy functioning (b1=0.073, p<0.001).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome grouping and category definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Group related health outcomes into broad categories (short‑term outcomes, long‑term outcomes, disease/symptom control) and into five specific analytic groups for heterogeneity exploration: (a) short‑term immune functioning, (b) short‑term endocrine response, (c) cardiovascular reactivity and physiological response, (d) long‑term promotion of healthy functioning, and (e) enhanced symptom control and survival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these groupings to compute aggregated effect sizes and to guide moderator analyses. Report which specific measures belong to each group (e.g., immune includes sIgA, T‑cell counts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of directionality for physiological measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret signs carefully: for some physiological outcomes (e.g., endocrine or cardiovascular reactivity), a negative relation between well‑being and the outcome is interpreted as promoting healthy functioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state interpretation conventions in tables/notes (e.g., 'a negative relation between well‑being and endocrine response should be interpreted as promoting healthy functioning because increases in stress hormones indicate compromised health').

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑independence caveat for comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not directly compare effect sizes that are not independent (e.g., across well‑being and ill‑being sections or across certain aggregated categories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note in tables when effect sizes are independent across study design but not independent across other sections; annotate that comparisons cannot be made when non‑independence exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling and reporting small subgroup findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise caution in interpreting moderator/subgroup results based on very small numbers of studies (e.g., single small study or K < 10 for that subgroup).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report sample sizes for subgroup analyses and explicitly caution against overinterpretation when subgroup N is small (example: unhealthy sample for endocrine response consisted of only one small study, N=26).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization of well‑being (state vs trait) as analytic factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Code and analyze whether well‑being was operationalized as a state (manipulated/measured transient affect) or as a trait (longer‑term SWB), because this distinction moderates effect sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report separate aggregated r for state and trait measures within each outcome domain; note patterns (e.g., state measures yielded higher immune functioning effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting study/sample descriptive characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide summary descriptors for included studies: number of independent samples per study, number of effect sizes per study, sample sizes (mean, median), participant age, gender composition, population sampled, funding source, country/site, year of report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tabulate these characteristics (e.g., Table II) and report skewness where relevant. Use these descriptors to inform moderator analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of BESD and practical interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Binomial Effect Size Display (BESD) to translate r effect sizes into easily interpretable practical terms (e.g., change in survival probability); convert BESD further to odds ratios (OR) and relative risks (RR) when helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide numerical BESD examples (e.g., r=0.14 → survival 57% vs 43%, OR=1.75, RR=0.75) and cite conversion procedures (Rosenthal & DiMatteo, 2001).

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance threshold and Z‑value conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat Z‑values with magnitude ≥ 1.96 as significant at p ≤ 0.05; report exact Z‑values alongside p‑values and CI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotate tables with this convention and mark effect sizes with Z≥1.96 as significant. Use standard p‑value notation (e.g., p < 0.001).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disaggregation by specific health measures when heterogeneity differs
rubrics_metrics.description: When heterogeneity varies across aggregated categories, disaggregate to examine specific health outcomes (e.g., immune functioning vs cardiovascular reactivity) because some outcomes show minimal heterogeneity and others show substantial heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report QBET to test whether specific health outcome explains heterogeneity; if significant, present separate aggregated effects for the specific measures (e.g., immune r=0.332, pain tolerance r=0.320).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about which effect model used for moderators
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about the statistical model used in each analysis: random‑effects for pooled estimates generally, fixed‑effects for meta‑regression of continuous moderators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight model choice in methods and in table footnotes; explain limitations (e.g., meta‑regression fixed‑effects assumption) and rationale for model selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding and counting of effect sizes and independent samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Define and report how many distinct effect sizes were computed and how many independent samples were coded per study; note ranges and distribution of effect counts per study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State coding rules for independence (e.g., one to six independent samples per study) and summarize central tendency (mean, median) and dispersion (SD) to show data structure feeding the meta‑analysis.
